text: Ingres was born into a modest family in Montauban and went to Paris to study in David's studio. He made his Salon debut in 1802. He wanted to guard academic orthodoxy against the rising Romantic style. He thought of himself as a history painter in the tradition of Poussin and David. Yet his portraits, painted and drawn, are what survive as his greatest legacy. His distortions of form and space influenced Matisse and Picasso.

Theodore Roussel came to painting late, in 1872, after his military service, and he was entirely self-taught. His first works were scenes of daily life in the style of the Old Masters. He moved to London in 1878. There he met James McNeill Whistler, who became a lifelong friend and mentor. At a New English Art Club show he caused a sensation with The Reading Girl, a life-size nude. He was a French-born English painter and graphic artist.

Joseph Wright of Derby specialised in portraits and landscapes. He is praised as the first professional painter to express the spirit of the Industrial Revolution. He used tenebrism, an exaggerated chiaroscuro that stresses the contrast of light and dark, and he often painted candle-lit scenes. Some of his paintings show the birth of science out of alchemy. Many were based on meetings of the Lunar Society of Birmingham, a group of scientists and industrialists. He lived from 1734 to 1797.

Tsuchida Bakusen was born on Sado island into a wealthy and influential family. His father put him on the path to becoming a Buddhist priest. He fled the temple where he was apprenticed to study art instead. Takeuchi Seihō accepted him as a student, and he later graduated from the Kyoto Kaiga Senmon Gakko in 1911. His younger brother was the philosopher Tsuchida Kyōson. Bakusen painted in the Nihonga style.

Jean-Léon Gérôme was born in Vesoul and became a painter and sculptor in the academic style. His paintings were reproduced so widely that he was arguably the world's most famous living artist by 1880. He painted historical scenes, portraits and Orientalist subjects, and he also took on Greek myths. With Meissonier and Cabanel, he was one of the three most successful artists of the Second Empire. He taught too. Mary Cassatt and Thomas Eakins were among his students.

Max Beckmann was born into a middle-class family in Leipzig. People call him an Expressionist, but he rejected both the word and the movement. In the 1920s he was linked to the New Objectivity, which opposed the introverted emotionalism of Expressionism. Even circus performers in his pictures carry an undercurrent of unease. By the 1930s his imagery had turned more horrifying, with distorted forms and social criticism, as Nazism rose in Germany. He also wrote.

Martin Johnson Heade was born in Lumberville, Pennsylvania, the son of a storekeeper. He studied with Edward Hicks. Possibly he studied with Thomas Hicks too. His earliest works were mostly portraits from the 1840s. As a young man he travelled to Europe several times, then became an itinerant artist at home. He is known for salt marsh landscapes, seascapes, and hummingbirds shown with orchids.

Simon Vouet rose to prominence in Italy before Louis XIII summoned him to France as Premier peintre du Roi. He and his studio made religious and mythological paintings, portraits, frescoes, tapestries and massive decorative schemes for the king and for rich patrons, Cardinal Richelieu among them. During those years he was indisputably the leading artist in Paris. He did a lot to bring the Italian Baroque style of painting to France. He lived from 1590 to 1649.

Carl Bloch was born in Copenhagen and studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Art under Wilhelm Marstrand. His parents wanted him to become a naval officer. He didn't. His only interest was drawing and painting. He went to Italy to study art, and on the way through the Netherlands he got to know the work of Rembrandt. He was Danish, and he died in 1890.

Raoul Dufy was born in Le Havre, the second of eleven children. His father was an accountant at a steel company and a talented musician. Dufy was a French painter linked to the Fauvist movement. His decorative style carried over into textile designs and public building decorations. He is most remembered for pictures of outdoor social gatherings. He also made prints and designed furniture.

Hans Memling was born in the Middle Rhine region and probably spent his childhood in Mainz. During his apprenticeship he moved to the Netherlands and spent time in the Brussels workshop of Rogier van der Weyden. He became a Bruges citizen in 1465. There he turned into one of the leading artists and master of a large workshop. A tax document from 1480 lists him among the wealthiest citizens. His religious works often include portraits of the donors who paid for them.

Justus Sustermans was court painter to the Medici family in Florence, and portraits of that family are what he is chiefly noted for. Emperor Ferdinand II invited him to Vienna to paint the Imperial family. He also gave Sustermans and his brothers patents of nobility. People celebrated him in his lifetime as the finest portrait painter in Italy. He painted history scenes, genre pictures, still lifes and animals too. He lived from 1597 to 1681.

Nicolas Cochin, called the Elder, was born at Troyes, the son of a painter. About 1635 he went to Paris. He often copied Jacques Callot and took Stefano della Bella as his model. Like them he was good at small figures, grouped with lively animation. His specialty was topography, including battles, sieges and encampments. Between 1676 and 1694 he engraved plates for the Grand Beaulieu, and he engraved the Siege of Arras with Jean Frosne.

Pieter Aertsen was called Lange Piet, Tall Pete, because of his height. He was born and died in Amsterdam, and he worked for a long time in Antwerp. He is credited with inventing the monumental genre scene, which joins still life and genre painting, often with a biblical scene in the background. His peasant scenes came a few years before the better known ones by Pieter Bruegel the Elder. They influenced later Flemish Baroque painting and Dutch still life.

Thomas Frye was born at Edenderry in Ireland and went to London as a young man to work as an artist. He is best known for portraits in oil and pastel and for early mezzotints. He also took out a patent for the Bow porcelain factory and managed it. His epitaph calls him the inventor and first manufacturer of porcelain in England, though Chelsea seems to have reached the market first. He retired to Wales in 1759.

Robert Campin is now usually identified with the Master of Flémalle. That name came from three panels said to have come from a monastery in Flémalle. Campin was a highly successful master painter, but no work can be certainly tied to him by a signature or document. A group of undated paintings has long been attributed to him. With Jan van Eyck, he started early Netherlandish painting. He died in 1444.

Elliott Daingerfield was born in Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, the son of a Confederate captain, and raised in Fayetteville, North Carolina. At 21 he moved to New York to study art and was apprenticed to Walter Satterlee. In 1884 he met George Inness. He studied in Europe around 1897 and was influenced by the Symbolists. He painted religious subjects, including a mural in the Church of Saint Mary the Virgin in New York. He became a full member of the National Academy of Design in 1906.

Giulio Campagnola was an Italian engraver and painter. His few, rare prints translated the oil painting style of Giorgione and the early Titian into engraving. He also invented the stipple technique, where many tiny dots or dashes make smooth gradations of tone, and that discovery mattered a great deal for later printmaking. He was the adoptive father of the artist Domenico Campagnola.

Elizabeth Nourse was born in Mt. Healthy, Ohio, near Cincinnati. She painted realist genre scenes, portraits and landscapes, and also worked in decorative painting and sculpture. She was the first American woman voted into the Société Nationale des Beaux-Arts. The French government bought one of her paintings for the Luxembourg Museum. Her contemporaries called her the dean of American woman painters in France.

Hasegawa Settan was born in Edo in the late Edo period. His given name was Munehide and his art name was Gengakusai Ichiyōsai. He was originally a wood sculptor, and he carved the woodblocks for many ukiyo-e prints. One of his major works is the Edo meisho zue, an illustrated catalogue of the sights of Edo, for which he made the woodcuts. He received the honorary Buddhist title Hokkyō for his accomplishments.

Lucas Cranach the Elder was court painter to the Electors of Saxony for most of his career. He was a close friend of Martin Luther, and eleven of his portraits of the reformer survive. He first painted religious subjects in the Catholic tradition, and later looked for new ways to convey Lutheran concerns. He kept painting nude subjects from mythology and religion throughout. His large workshop made many versions of his works, and his son Lucas Cranach the Younger kept making them for decades after his death in 1553.

Thomas Uwins was born in London and painted portraits, subjects, genre scenes and landscapes in watercolour and oil. He also illustrated books. He became a full member of the Old Watercolour Society and a Royal Academician. His appointments were high-profile ones. He served as librarian of the Royal Academy, Surveyor of Pictures to Queen Victoria and Keeper of the National Gallery. He died in 1857.

Merry-Joseph Blondel was a French history painter of the Neoclassical school. He won the Prix de Rome in 1803. He studied with Jean-Baptiste Regnault, and Ingres was a lifelong friend. Much of his career went to public commissions for paintings and frescoes, including work at Fontainebleau, Versailles and the Louvre, which kept him busy for decades. His 1814 painting La Circassienne au Bain became infamous. He taught at the École des Beaux-Arts until he died.

Gentile Bellini came from Venice's leading family of painters. At least early on he was rated more highly than his younger brother Giovanni, which is the reverse of today. From 1474 he was the official portrait artist for the Doges. He also painted very large works with many figures for the Scuole Grandi, the wealthy confraternities of Venice. Then in 1479 the Venetian government sent him to Constantinople. Sultan Mehmed II had asked for an artist, and his portrait of the Sultan was copied in paintings and prints across Europe.

Maximilien Luce was a French Neo-impressionist known for his paintings, his graphic art and his anarchist activism. He started as a wood-engraver and then concentrated on painting. First he was an Impressionist, then a Pointillist, and in the end he went back to Impressionism. He was born in 1858 and died in 1941.

Jeremiah Theus was born in Switzerland and became an American painter, mostly of portraits. He was active mainly around Charleston, South Carolina. For the bulk of his career he remained there almost without competition. He lived from 1716 to 1774.

Willem van Herp the Elder was born in Antwerp and worked there as a Flemish Baroque painter. He specialized in religious paintings and small cabinet paintings of low-life genre scenes. He ran a large workshop. Through his good connections with Antwerp art dealers he helped spread the Flemish Baroque style internationally. He died in 1677.

Abraham Govaerts was a Flemish painter who specialized in small forest landscapes in the manner of Jan Brueghel the Elder and Gillis van Coninxloo. He often worked with other artists who specialized in a genre. Govaerts painted the landscape while they painted the figures, animals or still life elements. He lived from 1589 to 1626.

Octave Tassaert was born and died in Paris. He painted portraits and genre, religious, historical and allegorical pictures, and he also worked as a lithographer and engraver. His genre pieces showed the miserable life of the downtrodden in Paris, including a number of scenes of suicide. He also made sensuous images of women, and erotic scenes. He wrote poetry too. His grandfather was the Flemish sculptor Jean-Pierre-Antoine Tassaert.

John Ruskin wrote about art and architecture, and about education and geology too. His forms were as varied as his topics. He wrote essays, verse, lectures and guides for travellers, and even a fairy tale, The King of the Golden River. He also made detailed sketches of rocks, plants and buildings. His early style was elaborate. Later he used plainer language to get his ideas across.

Hans Cranach worked in his father's workshop in Wittenberg next to his younger brother Lucas the Younger. His style was so close to his father's that the two are often told apart only by monogram, H.C. for Hans and L.C. for Lucas the Elder. Around 1537 he travelled to Italy and died unexpectedly in Bologna, at about 24. Luther mentions the death in his Table Talk, and a poet of the time, Johann Stigel, celebrated him as a painter.

Cardinal Alessandro Albani, a great collector of antiquities, backed Carlo Marchionni from the start and stayed his friend for life. Marchionni trained first as a sculptor, then studied architecture at Rome's Accademia di San Luca under Filippo Barigioni. In 1728 he won the academy's Concorso Clementino and caught Albani's eye. His early work for the Cardinal included the villa at Anzio and the papal retreat at Castel Gandolfo. His style sits on the cusp of Late Baroque and Neoclassicism. He died in Rome.

Five years under the marine painter Samuel Scott gave William Marlow his start. He also studied at the Saint Martin's Lane Academy in London. On the advice of the Duchess of Northumberland he travelled in France and Italy for three years in the 1760s. Back home he moved to Leicester Square. He painted marine and landscape scenes in oils and watercolours, with Richard Wilson and Canaletto as his models. His last Royal Academy picture, in 1807, was Twickenham Ferry by Moonlight.

Pietro Longhi took his surname only when he started to paint. His first teacher was Antonio Balestra, who sent him on to Giuseppe Maria Crespi in Bologna, a painter who knew Dutch genre pictures well. Longhi's first documented major work was an altarpiece for San Pellegrino in 1732. Eleven children came from his marriage, but only three grew up. In the late 1730s he turned to small genre scenes of Venetian life. Later writers called him the Venetian Hogarth.

A small shovel, a Schaufel, was the mark Hans Schäufelein put on his work, a pun on his name. He probably studied under Wohlgemut in Nuremberg and then assisted Dürer, whom he imitated. After a stint in Tyrol he collaborated with Hans Burgkmair on prints for Emperor Maximilian I, including woodcuts for the Theuerdank. In 1515 Nördlingen made him city painter. He kept the post for life. His output counts over 50 altarpieces and panels, and more than 1,200 woodcuts.

Jakob Bogdani came from Eperjes in northern Hungary, today Prešov, and his father was a painter. He went to Amsterdam in 1684 and to London in 1688. There he found success at the court of Queen Anne with still lifes and bird pictures. Several paintings entered the Royal Collection. Admiral George Churchill, whose aviary at Windsor Park may have supplied subjects, was a chief patron. Bogdani influenced the bird painter Marmaduke Cradock and died in Finchley.

Bartolomeo Schedoni's father made masks for the Farnese court in Parma, and the family moved there from Modena. He went to Rome in 1595 and apprenticed briefly with Federico Zuccari. His early work shows that he really studied Correggio in Parma. Twice he was jailed for fights. Between those episodes he served as court painter to Cesare d'Este in Modena. Later he worked for Duke Ranuccio I in Parma, who esteemed him greatly.

Georg Desmarées grew up in Stockholm, the son of immigrant parents, and learned to paint from a maternal relative, Martin Meytens. After Amsterdam and Nuremberg he reached Venice, where Giovanni Battista Piazzetta taught him. He married in 1731 and settled in Munich as a court painter. His wife died in 1743. He stayed in Munich until his death. A self-portrait and a portrait of his daughter survive.

Light saturation shaped the work of Santeri Salokivi. He studied at the Turku Drawing School from 1900 to 1904 and then in Munich and Paris. Later he taught in Turku and ran his own painting school in Helsinki in the early 1930s. His pictures include impressionistic archipelago scenes, figure compositions and finely made etchings. His name was Johansson until 1900. He is buried in the Hietaniemi Cemetery in Helsinki.

Paul Ranson's mother died giving birth to him, and his grandparents and his father, a mayor of Limoges, raised him. His grandfather gave him his first drawing lessons. At the Académie Julian he studied with Tony Robert-Fleury. In 1888 he became one of the five founders of Les Nabis, with Sérusier, Ibels, Bonnard and Denis. Japanese art, Japonisme, shaped his work strongly. He also wrote.

Corot was among the pupils of Jean-Victor Bertin, who taught landscape in Paris. Bertin's own teacher was Pierre-Henri de Valenciennes. From 1793 until he died he showed regularly at the Paris Salon. Palace commissions for the Trianon and Fontainebleau came his way in the 1810s. A gold medal followed in 1808 and the Légion d'honneur later. His last years brought money trouble.

Bartolo di Fredi painted the whole left aisle of the Collegiata in San Gimignano with a cycle of frescoes, signed and dated in 1367. He ran a large studio and was one of the most influential painters in Siena and its surrounding towns in the later fourteenth century. He joined the city's guild in 1355. In 1361 he helped decorate the Hall of Council in Siena. All his children died before him but one, Andrea di Bartolo.

Johann Liss left Holstein, studied in Haarlem and Amsterdam, and around 1620 travelled through Paris to Venice. His first works in Rome were influenced by Caravaggio. A move to Venice later changed that, bringing brilliant colour and a spirited, loose handling of paint. In 1627 he painted a much admired altarpiece, the Inspiration of Saint Jerome. Plague drove him out. He fled to Verona, and he died there.

Tessai was hard of hearing as a child, so his parents steered him toward scholarship rather than his father's trade in priestly robes. His father died when he was seven. He became a page at a Shinto shrine, and twelve years later he went to lodge with the Buddhist poet and nun Ōtagaki Rengetsu, his greatest mentor. In 1861 he opened a private painting school in her house. He is seen as the last major artist of the Bunjinga tradition.

Goethe learned to draw from Adam Friedrich Oeser, who stayed friends with him later in Weimar. Oeser studied sculpture and painting in Pressburg and Vienna, then went to Dresden in 1739. There he made portraits, scenes for the Royal Opera and wall paintings. In 1764 he became director of the new academy in Leipzig and fought mannerism. Winckelmann lived with his family for a time. Teaching was his chief importance.

Most of what is known about Jacometto Veneziano comes from the records of the diarist and art collector Marcantonio Michiel. From Michiel's testimony it seems he was mainly a manuscript illuminator and a painter of small panels, mostly portraits. He was active from 1472 to 1497. He died before 10 September 1497.

George Brookshaw began as a London cabinet-maker who decorated furniture with painted flowers. Later he published drawing manuals on fruit, flowers and birds, among them A New Treatise on Flower Painting, or, Every Lady Her Own Drawing Master in 1818. His 1812 book Pomona Britannica records fruit varieties grown in the gardens and greenhouses of Kensington Palace and other famous places. It is noted especially for its pineapples and cherries. He also used the name G. Brown.

Altarpieces were the business of Blasco de Grañén, who worked in Aragon from 1422 and became the painter to Juan II. In 1435 he made one for the Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar in Zaragoza. With his assistant Pedro García de Benavarre he did the altarpieces for the monastery of San Pedro de Siresa. He left the one for San Salvador in Ejea de los Caballeros unfinished at his death. His nephew Martín de Soria completed it. He followed Juan de Leví.

Around 1900 Jan Voerman painted the clouds above the IJssel river. He studied at the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam and then in Antwerp under Charles Verlat, and admired his contemporary George Hendrik Breitner. He was born in Kampen and died in Hattem, where the Voerman Museum shows many of his works. He married a daughter of the Verkade company founder. Their two sons both became illustrators. Voerman's work is also in the Rijksmuseum and the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum.

Elisabeth von Eicken built a house in Ahrenshoop in 1894 and lived beside the founders of the artists' colony there, such as Paul Müller-Kaempff and Anna Gerresheim. She came from Mülheim an der Ruhr, the third daughter of her family. After training in Merano, Menton, Geneva and Berlin she went to Paris to study with Edmond Yon. The Barbizon School and Alfred Sisley strongly influenced her landscapes. She showed in Berlin and at international exhibitions.

Willem van Bemmel left Utrecht, where he had studied under Herman Saftleven with his older brother Jacob, for Italy. He spent two years in Venice and about four in Rome, where he joined the Bentvueghels. After time in London he moved to Kassel for several years, and in 1662 he settled in Nuremberg, where he married. An engraver there, Christoph Wilhelm Bock, made his portrait. He painted Italianate landscapes. He died in Nuremberg at 78.

At 14, James MacDonald moved with his family from England to Hamilton, Ontario, and began his art training there under John Ireland and Arthur Heming. Two years later the family moved on to Toronto, where he studied commercial art and joined the Toronto Art Students' League, whose members believed in sketching outdoors. He later studied with George Agnew Reid and William Cruikshank. He joined the Group of Seven. His son Thoreau became an illustrator.

Parri Spinelli learned to paint from his father, Spinello Aretino, who worked all over Tuscany. For several years after 1411 he lived in Florence and belonged to the workshop of Lorenzo Ghiberti. When he came back to Arezzo he became its most important painter. His paintings have bold colors and figures more elongated than those of his predecessors. He died in 1453.

Cui Bai travelled to the capital Kaifeng to look for work as a court artist, and Emperor Shenzong, who admired his work, took him in. He was best known for paintings of animals and plants. He also gained a reputation for eccentric behavior. Two paintings are his main works today: Magpies and Hare, in the National Palace Museum in Taipei, and the handscroll Wintery Sparrow, in the Palace Museum in Beijing.

Theodore Earl Butler left Columbus, Ohio, for Paris to study art. In Giverny he befriended Claude Monet and married his stepdaughter Suzanne Hoschedé. After she died he married her sister Marthe. He painted domestic scenes of family and friends, and the French landscape. His Impressionist approach sometimes reflects his father-in-law, but his work also hints at Post-Impressionism. Butler was a founding member of the Society of Independent Artists..

Born in Bristol but raised in Dublin, Edwin Hayes went to sea for a spell as a seaman on a ship to America. He studied at the Dublin Society Art School and first showed at the Royal Hibernian Academy in 1842. In 1852 he moved to London, where he painted scenery at theatres like the Adelphi, as many young artists did. He became a full member of the Royal Institute of Painters in Watercolours in 1863. His seascapes nearly always have ships and boats in high seas or harbours.

Jan Steen's family ran a tavern in Leiden called The Red Halbert, and his father even leased him a brewery in Delft for a few years. Steen was the eldest of eight or more children and went to the Latin school, like Rembrandt. No official record of his training survives. Sources of his day name Nicolaes Knupfer, Adriaen van Ostade and Jan van Goyen as his teachers. His pictures are known for humour, psychological insight and satire of the Dutch middle class.

Jean Veber trained as a painter, but his brother Pierre urged him to join the staff of the newspaper Gil Blas, and he became an illustrator. In 1897 a drawing of Bismarck as a butcher of his own people caused a major controversy. He also drew for L'Assiette au Beurre and Le Rire. At fifty he volunteered for service in the First World War and was gassed. One critic noted that he never learned to be solemn.

Samuel Palmer painted churches from about twelve and showed Turner-inspired pictures at the Royal Academy at fourteen. He had little formal schooling or training. His mother died suddenly in 1818, and he wrote that it was like a sharp sword sent through the length of him. Through John Linnell he met William Blake in 1824, and Blake's influence shows in his work at Shoreham. He made visionary pastoral paintings and etchings, and he wrote a lot.

Cloudy skies, calm water and cattle fill the landscapes of Willem Roelofs, who is seen as a forerunner of the Hague school. He was born in Amsterdam, and his family moved to Utrecht. In 1839 they moved again to The Hague so that he could study at the academy and in the studio of Hendrik van de Sande Bakhuyzen. In 1847 he took part in founding the artists' society Pulchri Studio. His early landscapes are typical of the Barbizon school.

A trip to England in 1834 changed Jules Dupré. He was impressed by Constable, and the wide skies and water near Southampton and Plymouth taught him to paint movement in nature. He had first shown at the Salon in 1831. He leaned toward dramatic sunsets and stormy skies and seas. Late in life his handling grew larger and his colour simpler. He belonged to the Barbizon landscape painters.

Small, eerie canvases of gloomy ruins and crowded interiors, with elongated figures that seem to flicker, are the trademark of Alessandro Magnasco. He was born in Genoa, the son of a minor artist, and apprenticed with Valerio Castello and then Filippo Abbiati in Milan. He worked in Milan until 1735, apart from some years in Florence for Grand Duke Cosimo III. He often had other painters add figures to landscapes. His nickname was il Lissandrino.

Ker-Xavier Roussel studied at the Lycée Condorcet in Paris with his friend Édouard Vuillard, and the two also attended Diogène Maillart's studio. He frequented the Académie Julian, where Maurice Denis and others formed Les Nabis. In 1899 he travelled to northern Italy with Vuillard and Pierre Bonnard, and then settled at L'Étang-la-Ville. There he painted rural landscapes with nymphs, centaurs and fauns. His wife Marie, who was Vuillard's sister, and their children served as models.

Collectors' cabinets, rooms crowded with paintings and curiosities, were the subject that made Frans Francken the Younger popular, and they started a new genre. He painted big church altarpieces too, plus smaller historical and mythological scenes. He trained with his father, Frans the Elder, in Antwerp. He often worked with specialists in landscape, architecture and flower still life, adding the figures himself. He was the best known member of the large Francken family.

Woodcuts of broad black and white masses made Félix Vallotton known internationally. One series of ten interiors, Intimités, shows charged domestic encounters between men and women. He made few prints after 1901 and went back to painting. His later work includes finished portraits, nudes and landscapes painted from memory. His first paintings followed Holbein and Ingres. He also wrote art criticism in the 1890s.

Mushfiq worked in the atelier of Abd-ur-Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, the commander-in-chief of the Mughal army around 1600. He painted many pictures for the Ramayana and Razmnama manuscripts that the Khan-i-Khanan commissioned. Several individual paintings by his hand are known. Some are signed. As far as anyone knows, he did not work for the imperial workshops of Akbar or Jahangir. Some of his work is in the Freer Ramayana.

Reynolds ran a famously busy studio that turned out over 2,000 paintings in his lifetime. He promoted the Grand Style, which depends on idealising the imperfect. He was a founder and the first president of the Royal Academy of Arts, and George III knighted him in 1769. Lucy Peltz calls him the leading portrait artist of the 18th century. He specialised in portraits. He died in 1792.

Travels in Spain and Morocco in the 1880s sparked Théo van Rysselberghe's interest in light and colour. He came from Ghent, trained there and in Brussels, and at first painted in a realist and Orientalist style. He then turned to Neo-Impressionism. He was a founding member of the Belgian avant-garde group Les XX. His portraits and landscapes are known for a new treatment of colour and light. He helped link artists in Brussels and Paris.

Vasari is remembered for his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, which still sits behind many biographies of Leonardo and Michelangelo, though it contains many factual errors. He was a Mannerist painter and an architect, highly regarded in his own day and less so later. At the Medici court in Florence he was effectively a minister of culture. His Lives pushed the idea that Florence led the visual arts. He lived from 1511 to 1574.

Andrea Andreani cut woodblocks in Mantua and was among the first printmakers in Italy to use chiaroscuro, which needed several colours. His prints are scarce and valuable, and mostly copy Mantegna, Dürer, Parmigianino and Titian. Among the best are Mercury and Ignorance and the Deluge. He was active in Florence from 1584 to 1610. Museums such as the Met and the Cleveland Museum of Art hold his work.

Ishikawa Toyonobu may be the same person as Nishimura Shigenobu, since his earliest works are signed Nishimura Magosaburō Shigenobu. He studied under Nishimura Shigenaga. In the 1730s and 1740s he made many monochrome lacquer prints, showing the influence of Okumura Masanobu, mainly actor prints and pictures of beautiful women. He founded the Ishikawa Toyonobu school in Kyoto. His courtesans stand with the impassive faces typical of the Kaigetsudō school.

Surgeons ran in the Verhaghen family of Aarschot, but both sons chose painting. Pieter-Jozef's older brother Jan-Jozef became known as Potteke because he painted so many pots and bowls. Pieter-Jozef made large religious and mythological scenes and carried the tradition of Rubens into the late 18th century. He was appointed first court painter to Empress Maria Theresa, who gave him a stipend to travel abroad. He died in Leuven in 1811.
